title: A virgin shall conceive (Isaiah 7:14)
hook: the sign of a child named God with us, read by the Church as Christ

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah in the Temple, a coal on his lips, answering here am I, send me. Your line was here am I, send me. What did you volunteer for? Day four hundred sixteen.

A king stands at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, outside his city, with an invasion coming. His name is Ahaz, Achaz in the Douay-Rheims, king of Judah, and two neighboring kings have joined forces against him. The text says his heart shook like the trees of the forest in the wind. Then Isaiah comes out to meet him there and says: be calm. Don't be afraid. Their plan will not stand. And he makes an extraordinary offer: ask the Lord for a sign. Any sign. As deep as the underworld or as high as the sky. And Ahaz says, very piously, no thanks.
screen: `A KING BY THE UPPER POOL.` → `HIS HEART SHOOK LIKE TREES.` → `ASK FOR ANY SIGN. HE WON'T.`

segments.voice: Ahaz says, in the Douay: "I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord." It sounds humble. Isaiah hears it as a refusal to trust. So he says: then the Lord himself will give you a sign. "Behold a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel." Today's word. Emmanuel, in Hebrew immanu El: with us is God. Here, it's a sign for a frightened king: before this child is old enough to know right from wrong, the two kings you fear will be gone. Now, the part where readers differ, and it's worth knowing who says what. The Hebrew word Isaiah uses is almah, usually translated young woman. Jewish readers understand the sign as a child born in Ahaz's own time. The ancient Greek translation, the Septuagint, renders the word parthenos, virgin. And when Matthew's Gospel tells of Jesus's birth, it quotes this verse from the Greek: "Behold a virgin shall be with child, and bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us." The Catholic Church reads Isaiah's sign as finding its fullest meaning in Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, and Catholic tradition holds that a prophecy can speak to its own day and reach further at once. What everyone can see is the name. Not God far off. Not God above us. God with us, in the middle of a scared king's crisis, and, Christians believe, in a manger in Bethlehem.
screen: `I WILL NOT ASK.` · `IMMANU EL: WITH US IS GOD.` · `ALMAH, AND THEN PARTHENOS.` · `MATTHEW: GOD WITH US.` · then, large: `HIS NAME SHALL BE CALLED EMMANUEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say Emmanuel slowly. Settle, and breathe. Breathe in, and as you breathe out, say the first part, quietly: Emmanu. Breathe in again, and on the next breath out: El. Or say it in English: God, on the in-breath; with us, on the out-breath. Let it go slowly, like a heartbeat. If you pray, let it be a prayer: God with us, here, now. If you don't, let the words simply sit with you, and notice what it would mean not to be alone in whatever might be shaking you. The bell holds the time.
Emmanuel. Hebrew for God with us: the name of the child in Isaiah's sign, which Matthew's Gospel and the Church apply to Jesus. Today's word.
Your line: god with us. Today, at the moment you feel most alone, say the word Emmanuel once, under your breath. Day four hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Isaiah 7:14 in Advent and on the feast of the Annunciation, and in the last days before Christmas the Church sings the O Antiphons at Evening Prayer, among them O Emmanuel.

fork.setup: you're King Ahaz. two kings are coming against you, your heart is shaking, and a prophet says: ask the Lord for any sign you like. what do you do?
options: ask for a sign in the sky.
say, I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord.
ask Isaiah to choose the sign.
fork.reveal: Ahaz refuses, sounding pious. Isaiah answers that the Lord will give a sign anyway: a son called Emmanuel, God with us.

original.note: Hebrew: with us is God. Matthew translates it for his readers: God with us.

trapdoor: what you thought: Isaiah simply predicted the Christmas story.
what it means: a sign first given to a frightened king, which the Church reads as fulfilled most fully in Christ, born of Mary.
what a scholar hears: Hebrew almah, young woman; Septuagint parthenos, virgin. Jewish readers see a child of Ahaz's day; Matthew quotes the Greek.

notes: Almah / parthenos: the Jewish and Catholic readings are set side by side without ranking. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with the framing, including 'a prophecy can speak to its own day and reach further at once' (a common Catholic view, sometimes called the fuller sense).
The Septuagint is described as 'the Greek translation made before Christ'; the Isaiah portion is usually dated to the 2nd century BC. Confirm.
Ahaz trusting in a foreign empire (Assyria): from 2 Kings 16:7; confirm the hook's 'already decided'.
Isaiah 7:10–14 is read on the Annunciation (March 25) and the Fourth Sunday of Advent, Year A; the O Antiphon 'O Emmanuel' is December 23. Confirm.
CCC 497 cites Matthew 1:23 and Isaiah 7:14 on the virginal conception; confirm.
